claim: Fascin is an important regulator of F-actin bundling leading to enhanced filopodia assembly.
source: Fascin is an important regulator of F-actin bundling leading to enhanced filopodia assembly.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about fascin's function.

claim: Fascin is overexpressed in most solid tumours.
source: Fascin is also overexpressed in most solid tumours where it supports invasion through control of F-actin structures at the periphery and nuclear envelope.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about fascin expression in cancer.

claim: Fascin supports invasion through control of F-actin structures at the periphery and nuclear envelope.
source: Fascin is also overexpressed in most solid tumours where it supports invasion through control of F-actin structures at the periphery and nuclear envelope.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established function of fascin in tumours.

claim: Fascin has been identified in the nucleus of a broad range of cell types.
source: Recently, fascin has been identified in the nucleus of a broad range of cell types but the contributions of nuclear fascin to cancer cell behaviour remain unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a recent finding.

claim: Fascin bundles F-actin within the nucleus to support chromatin organisation and efficient DDR.
source: Here, we demonstrate that fascin bundles F-actin within the nucleus to support chromatin organisation and efficient DDR.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Fascin associates directly with phosphorylated Histone H3.
source: Fascin associates directly with phosphorylated Histone H3 leading to regulated levels of nuclear fascin to support these phenotypes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by FRET and immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Forcing nuclear fascin accumulation through the expression of nuclear-targeted fascin-specific nanobodies results in enhanced and sustained nuclear F-actin bundling.
source: Forcing nuclear fascin accumulation through the expression of nuclear-targeted fascin-specific nanobodies or inhibition of Histone H3 kinases results in enhanced and sustained nuclear F-actin bundling leading to reduced invasion, viability, and nuclear fascin-specific/driven apoptosis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data with nanobodies.

claim: Forcing nuclear fascin accumulation leads to reduced invasion.
source: Forcing nuclear fascin accumulation through the expression of nuclear-targeted fascin-specific nanobodies or inhibition of Histone H3 kinases results in enhanced and sustained nuclear F-actin bundling leading to reduced invasion, viability, and nuclear fascin-specific/driven apoptosis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by invasion assay data.

claim: Forcing nuclear fascin accumulation leads to reduced viability.
source: Forcing nuclear fascin accumulation through the expression of nuclear-targeted fascin-specific nanobodies or inhibition of Histone H3 kinases results in enhanced and sustained nuclear F-actin bundling leading to reduced invasion, viability, and nuclear fascin-specific/driven apoptosis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by viability assay data.

claim: Forcing nuclear fascin accumulation leads to nuclear fascin-specific/driven apoptosis.
source: Forcing nuclear fascin accumulation through the expression of nuclear-targeted fascin-specific nanobodies or inhibition of Histone H3 kinases results in enhanced and sustained nuclear F-actin bundling leading to reduced invasion, viability, and nuclear fascin-specific/driven apoptosis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by caspase 3 cleavage data.

claim: Fascin promotes the parallel bundling of actin filaments.
source: Fascin is an F-actin-binding protein that promotes the parallel bundling of actin filaments (Vignjevic et al., 2006a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Actin bundles formed by fascin can take the form of filopodia extending beyond the plasma membrane.
source: These actin bundles can take the form of filopodia (extending beyond the plasma membrane), or microspikes (within lamellae of migrating cells or neuronal growth cones) and are involved in numerous biological processes and pathologies (Hashimoto et al., 2011; Mattila and Lappalainen, 2008; Wood and Martin, 2002), including promoting cell migration (Adams, 2004) and during embryonic development (Zanet et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Actin bundles formed by fascin can take the form of microspikes within lamellae of migrating cells or neuronal growth cones.
source: These actin bundles can take the form of filopodia (extending beyond the plasma membrane), or microspikes (within lamellae of migrating cells or neuronal growth cones) and are involved in numerous biological processes and pathologies (Hashimoto et al., 2011; Mattila and Lappalainen, 2008; Wood and Martin, 2002), including promoting cell migration (Adams, 2004) and during embryonic development (Zanet et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Fascin expression is very low or absent in normal adult epithelia.
source: Importantly, fascin expression is very low or absent in normal adult epithelia, and a dramatic up-regulation at both gene and protein levels has been reported in the majority of human carcinomas studied to date (Hashimoto et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: A dramatic up-regulation of fascin at both gene and protein levels has been reported in the majority of human carcinomas studied to date.
source: Importantly, fascin expression is very low or absent in normal adult epithelia, and a dramatic up-regulation at both gene and protein levels has been reported in the majority of human carcinomas studied to date (Hashimoto et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Fascin is emerging as a key prognostic marker for metastatic disease.
source: Thus, fascin is emerging as a key prognostic marker and a potential therapeutic target for metastatic disease.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from previous findings.

claim: Fascin is a potential therapeutic target for metastatic disease.
source: Thus, fascin is emerging as a key prognostic marker and a potential therapeutic target for metastatic disease.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from previous findings.

claim: Loss of fascin function results in reduced migration and invasion in vivo across a range of cell types.
source: Across a range of cell types, loss of fascin function results in reduced migration and invasion in vivo (Chen et al., 2010; Hashimoto et al., 2007; Jayo et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2009; Zanet et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Fascin is made up of four β-trefoil repeats separated by short flexible linker regions.
source: Fascin is made up of four β-trefoil (βt) repeats separated by short flexible linker regions.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established structural knowledge.

claim: Biochemical and modelling data have identified N- and C-terminal actin-binding sites in fascin that enable efficient bundling activity.
source: Biochemical and modelling data have identified N- and C-terminal actin-binding sites in fascin that enable efficient bundling activity (Jansen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Protein kinase C (α/γ) phosphorylates the highly conserved S39 site within βt1 of fascin.
source: We and other groups have previously demonstrated that protein kinase C (α/γ) phosphorylates the highly conserved S39 site within βt1 of fascin and this negatively regulates actin bundling, cell protrusion assembly, and migration (Adams et al., 1999; Anilkumar et al., 2003; Hashimoto et al., 2007; Parsons and Adams, 2008; Vignjevic et al., 2006b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Phosphorylation of S39 in fascin negatively regulates actin bundling, cell protrusion assembly, and migration.
source: We and other groups have previously demonstrated that protein kinase C (α/γ) phosphorylates the highly conserved S39 site within βt1 of fascin and this negatively regulates actin bundling, cell protrusion assembly, and migration (Adams et al., 1999; Anilkumar et al., 2003; Hashimoto et al., 2007; Parsons and Adams, 2008; Vignjevic et al., 2006b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: S274 is a second conserved phosphorylated site in fascin that lies within the C-terminal actin-binding site.
source: We also identified S274 as a second conserved phosphorylated site that lies within the C-terminal actin-binding site that contributes to actin bundling and plays an additional role in the control of microtubule dynamics (Villari et al., 2015; Zanet et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: S274 contributes to actin bundling and plays an additional role in the control of microtubule dynamics.
source: We also identified S274 as a second conserved phosphorylated site that lies within the C-terminal actin-binding site that contributes to actin bundling and plays an additional role in the control of microtubule dynamics (Villari et al., 2015; Zanet et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Fascin is localised to the nuclear envelope where it binds directly to the nucleo-cytoplasmic linker protein nesprin-2.
source: Furthermore, we have shown that fascin is localised to the nuclear envelope (NE) where it binds directly to the nucleo-cytoplasmic linker protein nesprin-2 and regulates nuclear plasticity leading to enhanced cell invasion (Jayo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Fascin regulates nuclear plasticity leading to enhanced cell invasion.
source: Furthermore, we have shown that fascin is localised to the nuclear envelope (NE) where it binds directly to the nucleo-cytoplasmic linker protein nesprin-2 and regulates nuclear plasticity leading to enhanced cell invasion (Jayo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Fascin is located within the nucleus where it can bundle F-actin.
source: Additionally, we have demonstrated that fascin is located within the nucleus where it can bundle F-actin (Groen et al., 2015), but the role for nuclear-localised fascin and the potential impact on cancer cell behaviour remain unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: The nucleus contains high levels of actin, both monomeric and filamentous.
source: The nucleus contains high levels of actin, both monomeric and filamentous (Pederson, 2008), with actin filaments being shorter in length than those found in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Actin filaments in the nucleus are shorter in length than those found in the cytoplasm.
source: The nucleus contains high levels of actin, both monomeric and filamentous (Pederson, 2008), with actin filaments being shorter in length than those found in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Fascin is required for endogenous nuclear actin bundles to form.
source: Our data have shown that fascin is required for endogenous nuclear actin bundles to form, and depletion of fascin from Drosophila nurse cells increases the size and number of nucleoli, suggesting a role in maintaining nuclear actin organisation and compartments (Groen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Depletion of fascin from Drosophila nurse cells increases the size and number of nucleoli.
source: Our data have shown that fascin is required for endogenous nuclear actin bundles to form, and depletion of fascin from Drosophila nurse cells increases the size and number of nucleoli, suggesting a role in maintaining nuclear actin organisation and compartments (Groen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Transient actin filaments are detected in nuclei upon serum stimulation or cell spreading.
source: Transient actin filaments, detected in nuclei upon serum stimulation or cell spreading, are reported to regulate MAL (MRTF or MKL1) transcription factor activation (Baarlink et al., 2013; Plessner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Transient nuclear actin filaments regulate MAL (MRTF or MKL1) transcription factor activation.
source: Transient actin filaments, detected in nuclei upon serum stimulation or cell spreading, are reported to regulate MAL (MRTF or MKL1) transcription factor activation (Baarlink et al., 2013; Plessner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Endogenous fascin is localised to the nucleus in HeLa and MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: We further verified localisation of endogenous fascin to the nucleus in two human cancer cell lines, HeLa and MDA-MB-231 (used throughout this study), and validated specificity of staining using stable fascin knockdown (KD) cells in each case (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence images.

claim: In silico analysis identified putative bipartite NLS and NES sequences in fascin.
source: Our in silico analysis identified putative bipartite NLS and NES sequences (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in a figure.

claim: The NES mutant of fascin accumulates in the nucleus.
source: We mutated these sequences and performed biochemical fractionation analysis that demonstrated a clear nuclear accumulation of the NES mutant but not the NLS mutant (Figure 1A; Figure 1—source data 1), indicating that fascin is actively transported into and out of the nucleus.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data.

claim: Fascin is actively transported into and out of the nucleus.
source: We mutated these sequences and performed biochemical fractionation analysis that demonstrated a clear nuclear accumulation of the NES mutant but not the NLS mutant (Figure 1A; Figure 1—source data 1), indicating that fascin is actively transported into and out of the nucleus.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data showing differential localization of NES and NLS mutants.

claim: Treatment of cells with leptomycin B results in accumulation of nuclear fascin.
source: Moreover, treatment of cells with leptomycin B, which inhibits nuclear export through blocking exportin 1, also resulted in accumulation of nuclear fascin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence images.

claim: Deletion or mutation of any of the NLS residues in fascin led to loss of F-actin binding.
source: In our hands, however, deletion or mutation of any of the NLS residues led to loss of F-actin binding (not shown), which is perhaps unsurprising given the very close proximity to the crucial S39 residue required for actin bundling.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on experimental observations.

claim: Fascin-depleted cells show a striking loss of endogenous nuclear F-actin compared to controls.
source: Images demonstrated a striking loss of endogenous nuclear F-actin in fascin-depleted cells compared to controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence images.

claim: Expression of actin-NLS revealed long, crosslinked F-actin bundles decorated with endogenous fascin in control cells.
source: Expression of actin fused to an NLS and FLAG epitope tag (actin-NLS) revealed long, crosslinked F-actin bundles decorated with endogenous fascin in control cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence images.

claim: Assembly of nuclear actin-NLS-tagged filaments is markedly reduced in fascin KD cells.
source: Moreover, GFP-fascin expressed in fascin KD HeLa cells also colocalised with nuclear actin-NLS-tagged filaments and assembly of these filaments was markedly reduced in fascin KD cells within the same field of view (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence images.

claim: S39A fascin, which constitutively bundles F-actin, can induce nuclear F-actin bundles.
source: Further confirmation of the requirement for fascin-dependent nuclear F-actin assembly was demonstrated by data showing that S39A fascin, which constitutively bundles F-actin, could induce nuclear F-actin bundles, but the non-bundling mutant S39D could not (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence images.

claim: The non-bundling mutant S39D fascin cannot induce nuclear F-actin bundles.
source: Further confirmation of the requirement for fascin-dependent nuclear F-actin assembly was demonstrated by data showing that S39A fascin, which constitutively bundles F-actin, could induce nuclear F-actin bundles, but the non-bundling mutant S39D could not (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence images.

claim: Ratios of WT, S39A, and S39D fascin in nuclear vs. cytoplasmic fractions are very similar.
source: Ratios of WT, S39A, and S39D fascin in nuclear vs. cytoplasmic fractions were very similar (Figure 1A), indicating the differences in nuclear F-actin assembly were not due to variation in nuclear abundance of these proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data.

claim: Fascin is required for efficient nuclear F-actin bundling and this activity requires the N-terminal actin-binding site.
source: These data demonstrate that fascin is required for efficient nuclear F-actin bundling and this activity requires the N-terminal actin-binding site.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the S39 mutant experiments.

claim: Nuclear F-actin assembles in nuclei in re-spreading, post-mitotic cells to support nuclear expansion in early G1.
source: Previous studies have shown nuclear F-actin assembles in nuclei in re-spreading, post-mitotic cells to support nuclear expansion in early G1 (Baarlink et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation support.

claim: Fascin transiently localises to the nucleus following cytokinesis.
source: Live imaging of GFP-fascin cells identified that fascin transiently localised to the nucleus following cytokinesis.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by live imaging data.

claim: Nuclear F-actin transiently assembles post-mitosis in GFP-fascin cells.
source: In agreement with previous reports, nuclear F-actin was also found to transiently assemble post-mitosis in these cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by live imaging data.

claim: F-actin assembly is visibly impaired in fascin-depleted cells post-mitosis.
source: However, F-actin assembly was visibly impaired in fascin-depleted cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by live imaging data.

claim: There is a significant reduction in the duration of nuclear F-actin assembly post-mitosis in fascin KD cells.
source: Quantification confirmed a significant reduction in the duration of nuclear F-actin assembly post-mitosis in fascin KD cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification of live imaging data.

claim: There is a significant reduction in nuclear F-actin organisation in fascin-depleted cells.
source: Quantification of iRFP-nAC from post-mitotic cells revealed a significant reduction in nuclear F-actin organisation in fascin-depleted cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification of imaging data.

claim: Nuclear fascin is required to support efficient nuclear F-actin assembly.
source: This data collectively demonstrates a requirement for nuclear fascin to support efficient nuclear F-actin assembly.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the post-mitotic F-actin assembly experiments.

claim: Expression of Nb2-NLS results in enrichment of nuclear fascin.
source: We verified successful expression and expected relocation of endogenous fascin in cells expressing NLS and NES mCherry-Nb2 plasmids, with no change seen in endogenous fascin localisation in controls (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence images.

claim: Biochemical fractionation experiments confirmed the enrichment of nuclear fascin in cells expressing Nb2-NLS.
source: Biochemical fractionation experiments further confirmed the enrichment of nuclear fascin in cells expressing Nb2-NLS (Figure 2B and C; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data.

claim: Actin is the top hit across all Nb2 samples in proteomic analysis.
source: Data revealed actin as the top hit across all Nb2 samples, with Histones H3 and H4 the most highly represented proteins in the Nb2-NLS samples only (Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by proteomic data.

claim: Histones H3 and H4 are the most highly represented proteins in the Nb2-NLS samples only.
source: Data revealed actin as the top hit across all Nb2 samples, with Histones H3 and H4 the most highly represented proteins in the Nb2-NLS samples only (Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by proteomic data.

claim: Histone H3 associates with Nb2-NLS but not Nb2-NES.
source: Repeat GFP-Trap experiments verified the association of Histone H3 with Nb2-NLS but not Nb2-NES (Figure 2D; Figure 2—source data 3)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data.

claim: Endogenous fascin and Histone H3 partially colocalise within the nucleus.
source: and co-staining of cells for endogenous proteins revealed partial colocalisation within the nucleus (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence images.

claim: Fascin and Histone H3 can directly associate.
source: A range of FRET efficiencies were seen within a population of cells (Figure 2F and G), demonstrating that fascin and Histone H3 can directly associate and suggesting Histone H3 may act as a nuclear tether for fascin, contributing to fascin-dependent functions within this compartment.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by FRET data.

claim: Histone H3 may act as a nuclear tether for fascin.
source: A range of FRET efficiencies were seen within a population of cells (Figure 2F and G), demonstrating that fascin and Histone H3 can directly associate and suggesting Histone H3 may act as a nuclear tether for fascin, contributing to fascin-dependent functions within this compartment.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference from FRET data.

claim: There is a loss of Histone H3 binding to S39A fascin compared to WT or S39D fascin.
source: Subsequent probing of these complexes revealed a loss of Histone H3 binding to S39A fascin compared to WT or S39D fascin, indicating that fascin-dependent F-actin bundling reduces the interaction of fascin with Histone H3 (Figure 2H; Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data.

claim: Fascin-dependent F-actin bundling reduces the interaction of fascin with Histone H3.
source: Subsequent probing of these complexes revealed a loss of Histone H3 binding to S39A fascin compared to WT or S39D fascin, indicating that fascin-dependent F-actin bundling reduces the interaction of fascin with Histone H3 (Figure 2H; Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the S39 mutant binding experiments.

claim: Nuclear fascin binds to Histone H3 when not associated with F-actin.
source: Taken together these findings demonstrate that nuclear fascin binds to Histone H3 when not associated with F-actin and suggests a dynamic exchange of fascin within the nucleus that may act to coordinate nuclear organisation.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the binding experiments.

claim: Assembly of nuclear F-actin occurs following replication stress and induction of DNA damage.
source: Assembly of nuclear F-actin occurs following replication stress and induction of DNA damage, and acts under these settings to regulate nuclear volume, chromatin organisation, and oxidation status, driving efficient DNA repair (Belin et al., 2015; Lamm et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation support.

claim: Nuclear F-actin regulates nuclear volume, chromatin organisation, and oxidation status following DNA damage.
source: Assembly of nuclear F-actin occurs following replication stress and induction of DNA damage, and acts under these settings to regulate nuclear volume, chromatin organisation, and oxidation status, driving efficient DNA repair (Belin et al., 2015; Lamm et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation support.

claim: There is a significant reduction in the immediate recruitment of γH2AX to damaged DNA foci in fascin-depleted cells at 30 and 60 min post-NCS treatment.
source: Quantification of these data revealed a significant reduction in the immediate recruitment of γH2AX to damaged DNA foci in fascin-depleted cells (GFP) compared to GFP-fascin rescued cells at 30 and 60 min post-NCS treatment (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification of immunofluorescence data.

claim: γH2AX levels significantly reduce in fascin expressing cells 120 min post-NCS addition upon resolution of DSB.
source: Interestingly, γH2AX levels significantly reduced in fascin expressing cells 120 min post-NCS addition upon resolution of DSB; however, fascin KD cells remained at a significantly higher level indicating sustained DDR in these cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification of immunofluorescence data.

claim: Fascin KD cells exhibit reduced γH2AX levels compared to cells expressing WT fascin when treated with cisplatin.
source: When treated with the common chemotherapy drug cisplatin, which also induces DSB, fascin KD cells also exhibited reduced γH2AX levels compared to cells expressing WT fascin (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification of immunofluorescence data.

claim: There is enhanced γH2AX in nuclear fractions of NCS-treated GFP-fascin cells compared to fascin KD cells.
source: The reduced initial response to NCS in fascin-depleted cells was further verified in biochemically fractionated cells indicating enhanced γH2AX in nuclear fractions of NCS-treated GFP-fascin cells compared to fascin KD cells (Figure 3D; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data.

claim: GFP-fascin rescued cells show an increase in nuclear fascin and F-actin upon NCS treatment.
source: Further analysis of GFP-fascin rescued cells demonstrated an increase in nuclear fascin and F-actin upon NCS treatment (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence images.

claim: There is a significant increase in FRET efficiency in fascin expressing cells upon NCS treatment indicating enhanced chromatin compaction.
source: Lifetime images (Figure 3F) and FRET efficiency calculations (Figure 3G) revealed a significant increase in FRET efficiency in fascin expressing cells upon NCS treatment indicating enhanced chromatin compaction (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by FRET data.

claim: Fascin KD cells show basally enhanced chromatin compaction with no significant change upon NCS treatment.
source: However, fascin KD cells showed basally enhanced chromatin compaction with no significant change upon NCS treatment (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by FRET data.

claim: Fascin is required for chromatin organisation and efficient DDR.
source: These data demonstrate that fascin is required for chromatin organisation and efficient DDR.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the DDR experiments.

claim: Filopodia are significantly reduced in Nb2-NLS expressing cells compared to controls.
source: Filopodia were significantly reduced in Nb2-NLS expressing cells compared to controls, with no other changes seen in Nb2 or Nb2-NES expressing cells (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification of imaging data.

claim: Cells expressing Nb2-NLS show reduced migration speed on 2D surfaces.
source: Similarly, cells expressing Nb2-NLS showed reduced migration speed in cells on 2D surfaces (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification of live imaging data.

claim: Cells expressing Nb2-NLS show reduced invasion into 3D collagen gels.
source: and reduced invasion into 3D collagen gels (Figure 4D and E; note higher nuclei numbers in 0 µm Z-section images of the Nb2-NLS samples indicating fewer cells able to invade) compared to control cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification of invasion assay data.

claim: Nb2-NLS expressing cells exhibit a similar reduction in invasion to fascin KD cells.
source: Notably, Nb2-NLS expressing cells exhibited a similar reduction in invasion to fascin KD cells (Figure 4E), indicating that relocation of fascin to the nucleus prevents fascin function in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification of invasion assay data.

claim: Relocation of fascin to the nucleus prevents fascin function in the cytoplasm.
source: Notably, Nb2-NLS expressing cells exhibited a similar reduction in invasion to fascin KD cells (Figure 4E), indicating that relocation of fascin to the nucleus prevents fascin function in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the invasion assay data.

claim: Proliferation is significantly reduced in Nb2-NLS expressing cells compared to controls from 48 hr time periods onwards.
source: Proliferation was significantly reduced in Nb2-NLS expressing cells compared to controls from 48 hr time periods onwards (Figure 5A)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification of proliferation data.

claim: Reduced proliferation in Nb2-NLS expressing cells is coupled with a significant reduction in cell viability.
source: and this was coupled with a significant reduction in cell viability (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MTT assay data.

claim: A significant proportion of cells expressing Nb2-NLS accumulate in the G0/G1 phase of the cell cycle relative to controls.
source: Further analysis of DNA content 48 hr post-Nb2 induction revealed that a significant proportion of cells expressing Nb2-NLS accumulated in the G0/G1 phase of the cell cycle relative to controls.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by FACS analysis data.

claim: Nb2-NLS expressing cells exhibit reduced levels of S10 phosphorylated Histone H3 after 48 hr.
source: Nb2-NLS expressing cells also exhibited reduced levels of S10 phosphorylated Histone H3 after 48 hr (Figure 5D)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by quantification of immunofluorescence data.

claim: Nb2-NLS expressing cells show enhanced cleaved caspase 3 by 72 hr post-induction.
source: and enhanced cleaved caspase 3 by 72 hr post-induction (Figure 5E; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data.

claim: Enhanced and sustained nuclear fascin specifically induces cell cycle arrest resulting in reduced viability and enhanced apoptosis.
source: These findings collectively indicate that enhanced and sustained nuclear fascin specifically induces cell cycle arrest resulting in reduced viability and enhanced apoptosis.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the viability and apoptosis experiments.

claim: The mean RZ' of the neutral and positive controls in the high-content screen was 0.5017.
source: The mean RZ' of the neutral and positive controls in this screen was 0.5017, indicating excellent assay robustness.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a quality metric for the screen.

claim: 231 compounds were identified as hits in the primary screen.
source: Following quality control checks (e.g., to exclude images with very few cells), 231 compounds were identified as hits.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a summary of the primary screen.

claim: The mean RZ' of the compound response screen was 0.5607.
source: Data were analysed as for the primary screen (mean RZ'=0.5607)
evidence: This is stated in the results as a quality metric for the compound response screen.

claim: 96 compounds were identified as active against nuclear fascin in the compound response screen.
source: This compound response analysis identified 96 compounds that were active against nuclear fascin, of which 43 also increased nuclear F-actin.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a summary of the compound response screen.

claim: 43 compounds that were active against nuclear fascin also increased nuclear F-actin.
source: This compound response analysis identified 96 compounds that were active against nuclear fascin, of which 43 also increased nuclear F-actin.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a summary of the compound response screen.

claim: The most highly represented pathways targeted by compounds that increased nuclear fascin were cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDK).
source: The most highly represented pathways that were targeted by these compounds were cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDK).
evidence: This is stated in the results as a summary of the compound response screen.

claim: GSK3 was highly represented in the list of hits from the compound response screen.
source: The promiscuous kinase glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3) was also highly represented in the list of hits.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a summary of the compound response screen.

claim: 15 compounds promoted apoptosis at lower concentrations in mScarlet-fascin expressing cells than in fascin KD cells.
source: From these data, we identified 15 compounds that promoted apoptosis at lower concentrations in mScarlet-fascin expressing cells than in fascin KD cells, indicating dependence on enhanced and sustained nuclear fascin to drive apoptosis (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by apoptosis screen data.

claim: CDK2 inhibitor (SN0188025193), IRAK4 inhibitor (SN1047164129), and haspin inhibitor (SN1151669528, CHR-6494) exhibited a greater differential apoptotic effect in fascin-expressing vs. fascin KD cells.
source: We chose to follow up on three hits that targeted CDK2 (SN0188025193), IRAK4 (SN1047164129), and haspin (SN1151669528, CHR-6494), as these compounds not only exhibited a greater differential apoptotic effect in fascin-expressing vs. fascin KD cells, but also induced nuclear fascin and F-actin in both the primary and compound response screens

claim: Treatment with haspin inhibitor results in total loss of pT3-Histone H3 phosphorylation after 4 hr.

evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data.

claim: Treatment with IRAK4 inhibitor results in a reduction in pT3-Histone H3 phosphorylation after 8 hr.

claim: CDK2 inhibition after 4 hr does not directly alter Histone H3 phosphorylation.

claim: There is a striking reduction in fascin-Histone H3 association in cells treated with both IRAK4 and haspin inhibitors.

claim: CDK2 inhibitor does not reduce fascin-Histone H3 association.

claim: Analysis of immunoprecipitated GFP-fascin showed no change in fascin phosphorylation upon treatment with IRAK4, haspin, or CDK2 inhibitors.

evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data.

claim: IRAK4, haspin, and CDK2 kinases do not act directly to post-translationally modify fascin.
